content: The use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including fosfomycin (MONUROL), has been associated with the development of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD). The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Antibacterial treatments disrupt the normal flora of the colon, which can lead to an overgrowth of Clostridium difficile. Clostridium difficile produces toxins A and B, which are key contributors to the pathogenesis of CDAD. Certain hypervirulent strains of C. difficile produce higher levels of toxins, leading to increased morbidity and mortality. These infections may be resistant to standard antimicrobial therapy and, in severe cases, may necessitate surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in any patient presenting with diarrhea following the use of antibiotics. A thorough medical history is essential, as CDAD has been reported to occur even up to two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic therapy not specifically targeting C. difficile may be required. Clinical management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation when clinically indicated.
